desc:
iOS app maintenance and updates keep your iPhone app working as Apple releases new versions of iOS and Xcode. Ecom Swift LLC starts with a fixed care sprint: a build on current tools, compatibility fixes, library updates and a clean release build.

## What does iOS app maintenance involve?

iOS app maintenance is the regular work of keeping an app healthy after launch. It includes building the project on current Xcode, fixing warnings and deprecated code, updating libraries, repairing crashes, checking new device sizes and preparing a fresh release build for the App Store.

Software ages even when nobody touches it. Apple changes its tools every year, third-party libraries stop being updated and phones get new screens and settings. Maintenance deals with that drift before it turns into an emergency.

## Why apps break without anyone changing them

An app that worked at launch can start failing after an operating system update. A library may call a feature Apple has retired, a layout can shift on a new screen size, or an old permission request may stop showing. Users notice first, usually as crashes and one-star reviews.

Apple also expects apps to be built with recent tools and to declare how they use private data. An app left alone for a long time can find that it cannot be updated at all until a long list of old issues is resolved. A small, steady effort costs far less than that late catch-up.

## How maintenance protects your results

A stable app keeps its users and its ratings. Crashes are one of the most common reasons people uninstall, and a review that mentions a crash is read by every future visitor.

Maintenance also keeps your options open. With a clean build, you can ship a new feature, a bug fix or a seasonal change quickly. With a neglected project, even a one-line fix can take days because the build itself no longer works.

## What a good maintenance sprint includes

- A build on the latest Xcode, with a list of every warning and deprecation.
- Compatibility checks against the newest iOS and a few earlier versions.
- Review of crash logs and analytics for patterns.
- Updates to outdated libraries, with notes on any that are no longer supported.
- Fixes for the most urgent bugs and layout issues.
- A check of permissions and the privacy manifest.
- A look at memory use and slow screens.
- Removal of unused code and libraries that add weight.
- A written report with what was done, what remains and what to do next.

## How we work

We open your project, build it on current tools and list what breaks or looks risky. Then we fix the most important items, update what needs updating and test on several iOS versions and screen sizes. The result is a release build you can submit, and a report that tells you the state of the app in plain words.

The Basic package is a health check with the most urgent fixes. Standard adds more fixes, library upgrades and a tested release build. Premium adds performance, privacy and cleanup work and a care plan with a monthly quote if you want ongoing help.

This is a one-time sprint. Regular monthly care is quoted separately, and you are never locked in.

## Old libraries and ageing code

Sometimes a library has been abandoned by its authors. In that case we tell you the options: replace it with a current alternative, replace it with a small piece of native code, or keep it for now and plan the change. We explain the effort of each choice before we touch it.

## What to do, and what to avoid

**Do:**
- Keep a record of the Xcode version and tools the app was last built with.
- Update at least once a year, even without new features.
- Test on a recent iPhone before every release.
- Read crash reports as they arrive.
- Budget a small amount of time after each major iOS release.

**Avoid:**
- Waiting until an update is rejected before looking at the project.
- Updating every library in one step with no testing.
- Ignoring compiler warnings because the app still runs.
- Leaving secrets or old test code in the project.
- Treating maintenance as optional once the app has users.

## Who this is for

An owner who launched an app a year or two ago and has not opened the project since will benefit most. So will a business that inherited an app from a freelancer, and a team that is about to ship a new feature on top of an old codebase.

## What we need from you

We need the project repository through a collaborator invitation and any crash reports you have. If the sprint ends with a release build, we need a limited team role in App Store Connect. We never need your passwords, and we do not publish the update unless you ask us to.
